title: Proof By Induction
body:
Induction proves a claim $P(n)$ for **every** natural number $n$, using two finite pieces
of work. It is the technique for anything indexed by the naturals, which in computing means
anything recursive: [[Recursion]], [[Tree]] height, loop invariants, and the running time
of [[Merge Sort]].

The domino picture is the right one. Knock the first one over (base case), and prove that
any domino falling knocks the next one over (inductive step). You do not have to push
every domino, and that is the entire trick: two arguments cover infinitely many cases.

## The two parts

1. **Base case.** Prove $P(1)$ directly. (Or $P(0)$, or wherever the claim starts. Pick the
   smallest $n$ the claim is supposed to hold for.)
2. **Inductive step.** Assume $P(k)$ holds for an arbitrary $k$, and prove $P(k+1)$.

The assumption in step 2 is the **inductive hypothesis**. Assuming it is not circular
reasoning, and this is the thing everyone gets stuck on the first time. You are not
assuming what you want to prove. You are proving an *implication*:

$$P(k) \Rightarrow P(k+1)$$

That implication is a claim in its own right and you prove it outright. The base case then
supplies the one true instance the chain needs to start from. Neither half is worth
anything alone: without the base case you have proved a chain of dominoes with nothing
pushing the first one.

## Worked example

```
Claim:  1 + 2 + 3 + ... + n  =  n(n+1)/2   for all n ≥ 1

Base case (n = 1):
    LHS = 1
    RHS = 1(1+1)/2 = 1                          ✓

Inductive step:
    Assume  1 + 2 + ... + k = k(k+1)/2          ← inductive hypothesis
    Show    1 + 2 + ... + k + (k+1) = (k+1)(k+2)/2

    1 + 2 + ... + k + (k+1)
        = k(k+1)/2 + (k+1)                      ← by the hypothesis
        = k(k+1)/2 + 2(k+1)/2
        = (k+1)(k + 2)/2                        ✓

The claim holds for n = 1, and holds for k+1 whenever it holds for k,
so it holds for all n ≥ 1.  ∎
```

The shape is always this. The one line that matters is the one marked "by the hypothesis":
if your proof never uses the inductive hypothesis, you have not written an induction and
something is wrong.

## Strong induction

Ordinary induction assumes $P(k)$. **Strong induction** assumes all of
$P(1), P(2), \ldots, P(k)$ and proves $P(k+1)$ from whichever of them it needs.

Use it when the $n$ case does not reduce to the $n-1$ case but to some smaller case you
cannot name in advance. The standard example is that every integer $n \ge 2$ has a
[[Prime Number|prime]] factorisation: if $n$ is composite then $n = ab$ with $a, b < n$,
and you need the hypothesis at $a$ and $b$, not at $n-1$. Divide-and-conquer running times
are the same pattern: [[Merge Sort]] at $n$ leans on $n/2$.

The two are equally powerful. Strong induction is not a stronger *technique*, it is a
more convenient hypothesis.

## Structural induction

Induction over how a recursive object is **built** rather than over a number. Base case:
the atomic constructors. Inductive step: assume the property for the parts, prove it for
the thing assembled from them.

```
Claim: a binary tree with n nodes has n+1 null pointers.

Base:  the empty tree. 0 nodes, 1 null pointer.  ✓
Step:  a tree is a root plus two subtrees with n₁ and n₂ nodes.
       By hypothesis they have n₁+1 and n₂+1 nulls.
       The root consumes two of them (it points at the two subtrees)
       and adds itself: (n₁+1) + (n₂+1) = n₁+n₂+2 = n+1.  ✓
```

This is the version the COMP courses actually use, because the objects there are
[[Tree]]s, [[Context-Free Grammars|derivations]], and recursive functions rather than
numbers. [[Induction]] carries the short version of this.

## Where this is used

- [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTABILITY]]: every construction proof ("for any [[NFA]] there is
  an equivalent [[DFA]]") is an induction on the length of the input string.
- [[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]]: proving a recursive structure correct, and proving a bound in
  [[Asymptotic Analysis]]. Guess the closed form of a recurrence, then confirm it by
  induction; the guess is not the proof.
- [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER SCIENCE 2]]: [[Recursion]] and induction are the same idea
  pointed in opposite directions. A recursive function *computes* the way an inductive proof
  *argues*, and the base case is the same base case in both.

## Common ways to get it wrong

- Omitting the base case.
- Proving $P(k+1)$ without ever using $P(k)$: then you did not need induction, and you
  probably did not prove the general case either.
- Starting the base case at the wrong $n$. If the claim only holds for $n \ge 4$, prove
  $P(4)$, not $P(1)$.
- Assuming $P(n)$ for the specific $n$ you want, rather than an arbitrary $k$.
